extracted.intended_audience: general literate public; theatre-goers, authors, and readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance on effective stage acting (gesture, look, voice) and on authorship practices (use of fictitious letters, attribution, subject balance, and commercial honesty). Presented as observations, examples, and letters in a literary periodical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious variety in the countenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Countenance admits of so great Variety, it requires also great Judgment to govern it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not that the Form of the Face is to be shifted on every Occasion, lest it turn to Farce and Buffoonery; action (features and limbs) must conform itself always to the Sentiments of the Soul. Maintain appropriate variation without excess; avoid turning natural variety into caricature by over-changing facial expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness of the eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eyes have a wonderful Power of marking the Emotions of the Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use different kinds of looks (a stedfast Look, a careless one, a sudden Regard, a joyful Sparkling) to reflect the sense of the words as it is diversified. The eyes are a primary vehicle for conveying mental states on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture must conform to sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Action is, as it were, the Speech of the Features and Limbs, and must therefore conform itself always to the Sentiments of the Soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gestures should arise naturally from the character's feelings and the sense of the passage; they act as a universal tongue understood by all audiences. Avoid gestures that feel unrelated to the inner sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid farce/buffoonery by excessive change
rubrics_metrics.description: Not that the Form of the Face is to be shifted on every Occasion, lest it turn to Farce and Buffoonery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter facial expression or manner too frequently or gratuitously; excessive variation undermines sincerity and can reduce a performance to buffoonery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good sense is essential for good acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Without Good Sense no one can be a good Player, and he is very unfit to personate the Dignity of a Roman Hero, who cannot enter into the Rules for Pronunciation and Gesture delivered by a Roman Orator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors must possess common sense and comprehension of rules of pronunciation and gesture appropriate to the role; technical skill alone is insufficient without judgment and understanding of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right pitching of the voice (pitch control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Voice ... has its particular Medium and Compass, and the Sweetness of Speech consists in leading it through all the Variety of Tones naturally, and without touching any Extreme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find and work within the natural medium and compass of the voice; vary tones naturally without extremes. Anecdote: Gracchus used an ivory pipe to find pitch — metaphorically, 'Leave the Pipe at home, but carry the Sense of this Custom with you.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of look, voice, and gesture to move an audience
rubrics_metrics.description: lay wait not only for their superficial Applause, but also for insinuating into their Affections and Passions, by the artful Management of the Look, Voice, and Gesture of the Speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagecraft should aim beyond mere applause to touch audience emotions through coordinated use of glance, vocal modulation, and physical movement. This is an intentional, artful practice by performers and managers of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action, show, and dress permissible for entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Advantages of Action, Show, and Dress on these Occasions are allowable, because the Merit consists in being capable of imposing upon us to our Advantage and Entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenic and costuming devices are acceptable when they contribute to the audience's engagement and pleasure; the overall merit is judged by effectiveness in entertainment, though authors may resent when theatrical artifice masks literary weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious/pseudonymous letters by the author
rubrics_metrics.description: I often chuse this way of casting my Thoughts into a Letter ... First, out of the Policy of those who try their Jest upon another ... Secondly, because I would extort a little Praise ... Thirdly, because it gave me an Opportunity of introducing a great variety of Characters ... Fourthly, because the Dignity Spectatorial would have suffered ... And lastly, because they often serve to bring in, more naturally, such additional Reflections as have been placed at the End of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for publishing material under invented names: to test jests anonymously, to elicit praise from otherwise critical readers, to introduce varied characters and perspectives, to preserve the narrator's authority/dignity, and to provide a natural vehicle for reflective commentary. This is defended as a legitimate authorial device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider each paper as an independent tract
rubrics_metrics.description: I desire my Reader to consider every particular Paper or Discourse as a distinct Tract by itself, and independent of every thing that goes before or after it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers (and critics) should judge each essay on its own terms rather than expecting uniform subject-matter or constant line of argument across issues; avoids conflating pieces and misattributing intent across different papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance subject-matter between diversion and seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some affirm a Paper of this Nature should always turn upon diverting Subjects, and others ... find Fault with every one of them that hath not an immediate Tendency to the Advancement of Religion or Learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a recognized tension: papers may justly range from diverting to instructive, but the author warns that seriousness on an improper subject or levity in a serious subject will legitimately draw censure. Strive for appropriateness of tone to subject and moral intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial honesty in attribution and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: All that I was going to say about the Honesty of an Author in the Sale of his Ware, was that he ought to own all that he had borrowed from others, and lay in a clear light all that he gives his Spectators for their Money, with an Account of the first Manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should acknowledge borrowings and mark what is original vs. sourced; be transparent with readers about the provenance of material. The author claims to be scrupulous in quoting sources even when he might have made passages his own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial fairness in trade (seller's duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Philosopher made it a Rule of Trade, that your Profit ought to be the common Profit; and it is unjust to make any Step towards Gain, wherein the Gain of even those to whom you sell is not also consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchants should not conceal exceptions or defects; sellers ought to inform buyers of limitations when selling goods. Concealing faults or selling without disclosing exceptions is condemned as cheating; profit should not come at the buyer's unconsulted expense.
